locations.heading: 14.1.4. Cost of Append and Indexing #
locations.excerpt: 14.1.4. Cost of Append and Indexing # Dynamic arrays have two different stories: Reading items[index] is O(1) because the index points directly to the slot. Most appends are O(1), but an append that triggers resizing is O(n) because it copies existing values. Over many appends, doubling capacity gives amortized O(1) append cost. Amortized means the occasional expensive resize is spread across many cheap operations.

25.1.1. Compare Three Executions of the Same Dependency Rule # A repeated subproblem is a question with the same complete state, not just a similarly named function call. With F(0)=0, F(1)=1 and F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2), the integer n fully identifies the question. Fix that definition before sharing results. Changing the base values creates a different sequence and invalidates an old cache. For F(4), the naive call tree asks for F(3) and F(2). F(3) asks for F(2) and F(1), so F(2) is expanded twice. Termination is already guaranteed by decreasing n; the problem is repeated work. F(4)

locations.heading: 13.1.3. What an ADT Specifies #
locations.excerpt: 13.1.3. What an ADT Specifies # An ADT describes a set of values and the operations allowed on those values. It does not require one particular internal representation. For a stack, the contract might say: Operation Meaning Push(item) Add an item to the top. Pop() Remove and return the top item. Peek() Return the top item without removing it. Count Report how many items are stored. This contract says nothing about arrays or linked lists. That separation is the point: client code should depend on the behavior it needs, not on accidental implementation details.

locations.heading: 13.1.6. Contracts Include Rules #
locations.excerpt: 13.1.6. Contracts Include Rules # A contract includes more than method names. It also includes rules: Pop removes the same item that Peek would return. Count increases after Push and decreases after Pop . Pop and Peek on an empty stack are errors. A rule that must remain true for the object to be valid is called an invariant . Data-structure code often exists to preserve invariants while operations run quickly.

locations.heading: 14.1.4. Cost of Append and Indexing #
locations.excerpt: 14.1.4. Cost of Append and Indexing # Dynamic arrays have two different stories: Reading items[index] is O(1) because the index points directly to the slot. Most appends are O(1), but an append that triggers resizing is O(n) because it copies existing values. Over many appends, doubling capacity gives amortized O(1) append cost. Amortized means the occasional expensive resize is spread across many cheap operations.

addition of square brackets ( [] ) after the type specifier to denote it as an array.
So, the general form for declaring an array variable of the element type is: type [] variableName; For example, if you want to create an array called a with the type int for elements, you declare the array variable as: int[] a; In this declaration, you do not know how many elements will be in this array
from the preceding declaration. You must give further information to create the
corresponding array object . A new object can be created using the new syntax.

locations.excerpt: 20.2.4. Density and Workload Costs # For a simple undirected graph with V vertices, the maximum number of edges is V(V - 1) / 2 : choose an unordered pair of distinct endpoints. locations.heading: 24.3.3. Dijkstra with Nonnegative Directed Arcs #
locations.excerpt: 24.3.3. Dijkstra with Nonnegative Directed Arcs # Dijkstra minimizes path cost from one known source. A short checklist keeps the important questions from being skipped: Who is affected? List the stakeholders: users, customers, coworkers, the organization, and people outside it. What could happen, and how bad would it be? Consider likely and severe outcomes for each stakeholder. What do we owe them? greatest common divisor algorithm saves a step when we already have a and b in the right order . The right order means that \(a > b\) . As we noted earlier, the
cleverness of the mathematical definition is that a and b are
swapped as the first step to ensure that \(a > b\) , after which we can
repeatedly divide to get the GCD. Division, of course, is a form of repetitive subtraction, so the way
to divide by b is to repeatedly subtract it

locations.heading: 3.9.1. Who Owns Code #
locations.excerpt: 3.9.1. Who Owns Code # Code is a creative work, so copyright protects it automatically: you may not copy someone else’s code just because you can see it. A license is the owner’s permission to use the code under stated terms. Two common open-source examples: The MIT License is permissive : anyone may use, copy, modify, and sell the code, as long as they keep the copyright and license notice. [ 1 ] The GNU General Public License (GPL) is copyleft : if you distribute a modified version, you must release it under the GPL as well. [ 2 ] Code written for an employer usually belongs to the employer. Code with no license at all is not free to reuse.

locations.excerpt: 13.4.6. Iterators Are Lazy # An iterator method does not run its body when you call it — it runs one step at a time, only as far as the caller actually asks for elements. Calling EvenNumbers(1, 1000000) returns instantly; the loop body only executes as foreach requests each next value. This matters for two reasons: an iterator can describe an infinite or unbounded sequence without ever running forever, and a foreach that stops early (with break ) never computes the elements it never asked for.

locations.heading: 24.2.5. Kruskal Invariants and the Cut Argument #
locations.excerpt: 24.2.5. Kruskal Invariants and the Cut Argument # Accepted edges are acyclic. Union-find tracks exactly the components connected by accepted edges; an edge with equal roots would create a cycle. A minimum-cost crossing edge is safe: take the cut separating one current component from the rest. An optimal spanning forest that lacks the chosen edge can exchange a crossing edge on the resulting cycle for it without raising cost. Within each connected input component, this cut argument shows the accepted forest can be extended to an optimum. Acyclicity alone would not prove minimality. The implementation uses union by size and path halving. Sortin

class, and method names and camelCase for variable and
method parameters. [ 2 ] Use meaningful and descriptive names for variables, methods, and classes. Avoid keywords when naming identifiers (see Section 1.3 ).

locations.heading: 18.3.4. Priority Is Different from Fairness #
locations.excerpt: 18.3.4. Priority Is Different from Fairness # A strict priority rule may postpone low-priority work indefinitely when urgent work keeps arriving. Stable arrival ties solve ordering among equal priorities, not fairness between priority levels. Choose a business rule for escalation or bounded urgent service before claiming a scheduler is fair. For top-k, state whether duplicates count as separate observations, what k=0 means, and how results are finally displayed. Maintaining a heap of at most k retained values costs O(k) storage and O(log k) repair per retained update; producing a sorted output is additional work.

locations.excerpt: 8.2.4.5. Processing Order # Sometimes the important question is which item should leave the collection next. If urgency should take precedence, make the urgency rule explicit and choose a different structure.

locations.heading: 11.4.5. Refactor Without Changing the Contract #
locations.excerpt: 11.4.5. Refactor Without Changing the Contract # Refactoring changes internal organization while preserving intended observable behavior. Suppose a console program keeps product names, prices, and quantities in parallel lists. Each insertion must update all three lists in the same order, so a missing update can silently pair the wrong price with a product. First capture a few expected orders as checks. Keep the public task the same: add requested products and obtain the correct total. Run the checks after each small change.

locations.excerpt: 18.2.1. Repair Only the Part an Operation Can Disturb # Enqueue adds a new entry at the next open leaf position so the complete shape is preserved. Moving upward strictly decreases its index, so repair terminates. Start with [2, 5, 4] and enqueue 1. Appending produces [2, 5, 4, 1]. Comparing 1 with parent 5 gives [2, 1, 4, 5]. Comparing that 1 with root 2 gives [1, 2, 4, 5]. Do not sort the whole array; that would enforce a stronger and more expensive condi

locations.excerpt: 23.1.5. Repeated-Query Workloads # For q lookups, scanning costs up to Θ(qn). Sorting once and searching costs Θ(n log n+q log n), assuming a comparison sort and static data. Updates can invalidate the sorted snapshot or require maintenance. Sorting merely to answer one query may add work; an existing sorted array can support binary search even for one query. Dictionary exact-key lookup needs its own duplicate and update policy; ordered ranges and all matches are different requirements.

locations.excerpt: 15.1.1. Stack Behavior # A stack is an abstract data type where the most recently added item is the next item removed. This access rule is called last in, first out , or LIFO . Count reports how many values are currently stored. The point of a stack is not that it stores data in a new magical way. locations.heading: 6.4.3. Thinking Through an Ethical Question #
locations.excerpt: 6.4.3. Thinking Through an Ethical Question # Ethical decisions in software are rarely about villains. They are usually about trade-offs under deadline pressure. A short checklist keeps the important questions from being skipped: Who is affected? List the stakeholders: users, customers, coworkers, the organization, and people outside it. What could happen, and how bad would it be? Consider likely and severe outcomes for each stakeholder. What do we owe them? Consider laws, contracts, promises made to customers, and professional codes. Could we explain this decision publicly? If a decision only works while nobody knows about it, reconsider it.

locations.heading: 5.2.2. Variable Scopes #
locations.excerpt:
5.2.2. Variable Scopes # A variable may be available for use in some parts of code, but not others.
The scope of a variable is the region of the program that the variable is visible,
which means it is accessible by name and can be used in the part of code. C# scope rules of variables can be divided into three categories as follows: Class Level Scope Method Level Scope Block Level Scope. A variable declared inside a method is a local variable . A body local belongs to its containing block; a parameter is available in the method body. A nested-block local cannot be used outside that block. You cannot use a local variable before its declaration

locations.excerpt: 3.1. Why Use Version Control # Version control gives you a record of your work that you can inspect, undo, and share. locations.heading: 13.1.3. What an ADT Specifies #
locations.excerpt: 13.1.3. What an ADT Specifies # An ADT describes a set of values and the operations allowed on those values. It does not require one particular internal representation. For a stack, the contract might say: Operation Meaning Push(item) Add an item to the top. Pop() Remove and return the top item. Peek() Return the top item without removing it. Count Report how many items are stored. This contract says nothing about arrays or linked lists. That separation is the point: client code should depend on the behavior it needs, not on accidental implementation details.

locations.excerpt: 14.1.9. Why Doubling Gives Amortized Constant Cost # For nine appends, the trace copies 2 + 4 + 8 = 14 existing entries and writes nine new entries. Counting these array writes gives 23 writes across nine operations. Some individual appends are costly, but the total grows in proportion to the number of appends. For a longer sequence, copy sizes form 2 + 4 + 8 + ... . Each term is twice the previous one, so the sum stays below twice the final number of inserted items. locations.excerpt:
2.4.3. Output # In a regular C# program, including the VS Code projects used in this book, values are not displayed just because an expression exists in the source code. You must explicitly give the program an instruction to print to the console or terminal. This printing is accomplished through a method with a long name: Console.WriteLine .
Like with math, you can pass a method a value to work on, by placing it in
parentheses after the name of the method. Console is a C# class maintained by the system, that
interacts with the terminal or console window where text output
appears for the program. A method defined in that class is WriteLine .
